articles.title: A quarterback earns another useful assignment
articles.dek: Lavender and Cerulean found different ways to keep asking something manageable of their passers. Trust showed up in the next call.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Travis Scarboro was asked whether Frosmoth had done enough in Lavender’s 13–3 win over Azalea. “We won,” he said. When the question turned to the next quarterback decision, he added, “We’ll evaluate it.” Anyone hoping to leave with a dramatic declaration had chosen the wrong interview. Asking him about a particular possession was more productive.

“There were throws that kept us on the field,” Scarboro said. “There were possessions we need to finish better. Those are separate evaluations.” I prefer that answer to the sudden coronations that tend to follow a replacement quarterback’s victory. Frosmoth completed eighteen of thirty-four passes for 162 yards, one touchdown and no interceptions. He helped Lavender reach 8–5. He also has more work available than a simple winning record can describe.

Mr. Clanky’s reported recovery counter has reached zero. That is an availability development, and the next starting assignment remains a separate decision. Lavender can assess the alternatives without retroactively reducing Frosmoth’s contribution to a holding action. The Wails needed the football looked after, enough useful completions to support their defense, and a scoring drive when the game was still waiting for someone to take charge. He supplied those things.

I find the distinction useful because Cerulean spent the same week showing a more dramatic version of trust. The Tide beat Cinnabar 18–17 after a final touchdown drive and a successful two-point try. Their quarterback, Farigiraf, had to keep throwing after an unsuccessful play threatened to end the afternoon. Lavender and Cerulean won different games, but both gave their passers another clear assignment when the previous series had become frustrating.
Lavender’s modest requests

Lavender’s touchdown came on a nine-play, seventy-one-yard possession beginning with 4:47 left in the second quarter. Frosmoth finished it with a four-yard throw short right to Beedrill on second-and-two. The score was small in distance and large in consequence. Neither side had scored before it, and Azalea never reached the end zone afterward.

The Wails did not need to spend the rest of the game proving that every possession could resemble that one. They added a forty-five-yard field-goal drive after halftime and a sixty-six-yard field-goal drive in the fourth quarter. Just a cactus made both attempts, from thirty-nine and thirty-two yards, and his extra point. A quarterback’s useful work includes moving the team into range for somebody else to complete the job.

There is a limit to the comfort in that sentence. Lavender punted five times and converted four of eleven third downs. A team with postseason ambitions will want more than thirteen points often enough that the staff should continue asking hard questions. Yet demanding improvement is compatible with recognizing the practical help a passer has already provided. Frosmoth’s zero interceptions mattered in a game where one touchdown was the difference between the two offenses.

Scarboro’s defense allowed Azalea one conversion in ten third-down attempts. That gave the offense repeated chances to find enough points. It also gave the coaches a reason to value ball security without treating caution as a complete offensive plan. Lavender still had to advance the ball. The long fourth-quarter possession, thirteen plays and nearly three minutes, was substantial work even though it ended in a field goal.
Cerulean asks again

Farigiraf’s situation at Cerulean was less forgiving. The Tide trailed 17–10 when their last touchdown possession began with 1:45 remaining. At 1:39, Gumshoos sacked him on third-and-two. A few seconds later, on fourth-and-ten, Farigiraf found number 35 Watchog deep right for nineteen yards. Cerulean had asked its quarterback to rescue the possession immediately after the sack, and he did.

“I thought they might be tired of seeing us by then,” Farigiraf said. “We decided to stay a little longer.” There was a playful edge to the answer, but very little spare time in the drive. Arctozolt gained seventeen on third-and-eight. Prinplup then became a repeated target on the right, catching passes for six, six, eight and fifteen yards during the possession. Farigiraf kept finding a way to give the next player something useful to do.

Prinplup caught all four of his targets for thirty-five yards. Asked about being called on so often at the end, he said, “Four passes, four catches. I’m happy to discuss which part was confusing.” There is a pleasing directness to that sort of receiver confidence. It gives a quarterback somewhere to look while everyone else is calculating how much time remains.

Number 35 Watchog caught the four-yard touchdown, and Farigiraf found Arctozolt short right for the two-point conversion. The Tide moved ahead 18–17. Cinnabar still reached a fifty-four-yard field-goal attempt, which missed wide left. Cerulean’s victory required its own late execution and one final unsuccessful kick by the opposition; both belong in the account.
Keep the praise specific

I would resist turning either result into a grand verdict on quarterback identity. Frosmoth’s next role is still a coaching decision. Farigiraf’s two touchdown passes did not erase six Cerulean punts or a blocked punt returned for a Cinnabar touchdown. Both teams had enough uneven possessions to keep the review busy. The performances became valuable through particular responses to those difficulties.

For Lavender, the praise can begin with the seventy-one-yard touchdown drive, the absence of interceptions and the fourth-quarter advance into field-goal range. For Cerulean, it can begin with the fourth-and-ten conversion and continue through the repeated completions to Prinplup. Those descriptions give players something they can recognize and attempt again. A vague announcement that a quarterback has finally become a winner gives him much less practical help.

The two clubs also carry different pressures into next week. Lavender hosts Celadon from a position of relative strength at 8–5. Cerulean visits Azalea at 6–7, with every result carrying weight in its effort to remain among the conference’s postseason contenders. Neither has earned the luxury of treating a good final score as the end of the evaluation.

I would like Scarboro to keep asking Frosmoth questions about the actual throws. I would like Cerulean to remember that number 35 Watchog’s nineteen-yard catch came immediately after a sack, with the game nearly gone. A passer can be corrected and still receive the next important assignment. Farigiraf got one on fourth-and-ten; Lavender’s staff has its own set of decisions to make before Celadon arrives.

articles.title: Crasher Wake, give that defense another touchdown
articles.dek: Pastoria sacked Eterna seven times and won 10–3. A team that can do that deserves more reliable help from its own offense.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Crasher Wake, I watched your defense sack the opposing quarterback seven times. I watched your offense finish with ten points. I am prepared to compliment one of those performances at considerable length, and I am prepared to ask the other side of the ball why the celebration needed to remain so nervous for so long.

Pastoria beat Eterna 10–3 and moved to 6–7. That is a useful win over a division leader, earned through a defense that repeatedly made the next passing down more difficult. The Waves have a reason to keep talking about the postseason. They also have a responsibility to make better use of the possessions their defense is buying. Seven sacks should purchase a little breathing room.

The winning touchdown drive finally arrived in the fourth quarter. Togekiss threw for 181 yards and one score without an interception. Farigiraf caught six passes for sixty-two yards, including the six-yard touchdown. Kilowattrel added sixty-one yards on three receptions. Those are real contributions, and I will name them before anybody accuses me of ignoring the offense entirely. I am asking for more because the useful pieces were visible.

Pastoria finished with 234 total yards. The rushing attack produced fifty-three on twenty-three attempts. Watchog carried eighteen times for forty-five yards. The Waves converted four of ten third downs and punted four times. An offense can win a particular game with those figures, as Pastoria has kindly demonstrated. Depending on that level of production every week gives the defense a very expensive assignment.
The defense created the opening

At the beginning of the fourth quarter, the opposing quarterback was sacked on consecutive plays. Aggron took him down for seven yards, and Krookodile followed with another seven-yard sack. Rapidash then returned the punt twenty-one yards. Pastoria’s next possession began with a chance to travel forty-three yards for the lead. The defense and return game had supplied an excellent invitation.

The first two offensive plays gained nothing. Watchog was stopped up the middle, and a deep-left pass intended for Seviper fell incomplete. Then Togekiss found Kilowattrel deep right for twenty-seven yards on third-and-ten. There is the play I want the coaching staff to spend time on. The Waves needed a substantial gain, and the quarterback and receiver supplied one at the exact moment the possession was threatening to become another punt.

Kilowattrel later gained eleven on a short-left throw. Farigiraf finished the drive with a six-yard touchdown reception short right at 4:06. Horsea’s extra point made it 10–3. That six-play possession contained different depths, different targets and enough completion value to overcome the empty opening snaps. Pastoria should investigate how to make those elements available earlier in games.

“I want the next one faster,” Togekiss said. “We had the chances. I’m already thinking about where we can get the ball out and keep moving.” That is an answer I appreciate from a quarterback. He can enjoy the victory and remain impatient with the possessions that made it difficult. Nobody is demanding an apology for winning. I am demanding that the next week’s preparation acknowledge how much work the defense performed.
The closeout still needed rescue

After taking the lead, Pastoria had an opportunity to improve its position with another possession. Three Watchog runs produced no gain, no gain and a one-yard loss. Horsea punted. The Waves handed their defense another one-score situation with the game still available to the opponent. A unit that had already supplied so much now had to finish the argument itself.

The defense did. Drednaw sacked the quarterback for seven yards on third-and-ten with 1:10 remaining. Nidorina then broke up the fourth-and-seventeen throw. Pastoria regained possession, and Watchog eventually supplied an eleven-yard run before the closing kneel. The last necessary rushing gain arrived. I would have preferred one on the previous possession, when three unsuccessful attempts made the defense go back out.

That does not require deciding that every run was a bad call. It requires asking what the offense can reasonably expect from a sequence of calls in that situation. Pastoria had just scored by completing meaningful passes, including a third-and-ten conversion. Its next series gained minus one yard on the ground. The coaches should examine the available alternatives with more care than a general instruction to protect the lead.

Farigiraf had a suitably mischievous answer when asked about his touchdown. “I thought seven points might improve the mood,” he said. It did. The receiver caught six of eight targets and gave Togekiss a useful presence throughout the game. Kilowattrel, quieter about his own work, said, “I knew the third down mattered. I wanted the catch to be the part people remembered.” Pastoria has enough material for an offensive review that includes successful answers.
Ten points should be the beginning

The Waves have scored 144 points in thirteen games and allowed 190. Those season totals explain why one efficient fourth-quarter drive should be treated as something to build from. The defense has just shown it can produce a game worthy of a contender. The offense has to make that performance less dependent on repeatedly winning the final difficult down.

Horsea contributed a fifty-yard field goal in the second quarter and the extra point after the touchdown. Pastoria’s scoring depended on a long kick and a single touchdown drive. I admire a kicker who does his job from fifty. I would also like the rest of the offense to give him more routine extra-point work. An accurate long field goal is valuable; needing one to account for most of the first three quarters is a demanding arrangement.

Petalburg visits next after being shut out at Mossdeep. Pastoria should expect a Pride team with a great deal to correct and every reason to want an immediate response. The Waves have their own clear assignment: turn more of their productive completions into sustained scoring possessions. They cannot assume that another opponent will remain stuck on three points while they search for their second score.

Crasher Wake can begin that preparation with the twenty-seven-yard completion to Kilowattrel, the eleven-yard follow-up and Farigiraf’s touchdown. He can place those plays beside the three-run possession that followed and ask which choices give his offense the best chance to stay on the field. The defense has delivered its evidence. Pastoria’s next scoring drive needs to arrive before the fourth quarter requires another rescue.

articles.title: The Rook Board: start with the job each club needs filled
articles.dek: Fortree compares protection with coverage, Eterna needs offensive help, and all 32 clubs get a first scouting agenda before the offseason changes it.
articles.author: calvin-rook

body.text: Fortree should spend its first serious draft meeting comparing protection with coverage. The Skyhawks have taken forty-six sacks and allowed 341 points through thirteen games. I ranked Marshadow first on last week’s board, and I still want Fortree to study him. I also want Agate State’s Lapras in the conversation before anyone decides that a spectacular defensive-back workout automatically ends the discussion.

This week’s board asks which jobs each club should investigate. The priorities are my judgments from visible production, recorded games and confirmed availability. Team totals identify questions; they do not assign every sack to an offensive lineman or every conceded point to a cornerback. A useful scouting meeting compares the possible causes, the available prospects and the role the newcomer would actually receive.
Fortree’s two expensive problems

Marshadow’s 85–99 scouting band, 4.55 forty and 6.10 cone justify serious attention at cornerback. The Gateon State prospect leads my current board because the combination is unusually attractive. Fortree has just followed a seventy-nine-point defeat with a much more competitive 29–23 loss. Coverage remains worth improving even after a better afternoon, and the first game does not establish exactly which defender a rookie should replace.

Lapras offers a different answer. Agate State’s offensive-line prospect has a 77–99 band, a 4.95 forty and seventeen bench repetitions. Those numbers earn an examination of the protection job. They do not prove that Lapras can eliminate sacks, because quarterback decisions, receiver availability and the opponent’s rush all affect the result. Forty-six sacks are still enough reason for Fortree to make the examination a priority.

I would put Marshadow and Lapras through the work their proposed jobs demand, then compare the improvement available at each position. That is a better draft argument than announcing that the team with the worse defense must always choose a defender. The Skyhawks need both sides to become more dependable, and the best available improvement may depend on which player is actually within reach when their selection arrives.
Contenders can plan beyond this week

Mossdeep has scored 597 points and allowed 117. A team with that production can be selective about the developmental role it creates. The continuing absences of cornerback Marshall Flock and safety Luvrelle Revis make secondary depth a reasonable investigation, while the offense’s sustained success makes future protection worth preserving. Neither concern implies that the Eclipse should replace a successful starter simply to give a prospect an impressive label.

Saffron and Mt. Silver have similar freedom to examine succession with patience. Saffron has made fifty sacks and allowed fourteen; the Reds have allowed only 105 points. Those results should make a club more careful about displacing useful players. A rookie needs a real opportunity to become useful. Carrying an attractive prospect without a credible job is a considerably less exciting plan once the first practice arrives.

Sunyshore’s new Serp Gardener absence puts coverage depth in the current conversation. The draft is a later decision, and a two-week injury counter cannot decide the entire next season. Karson Jones should ask whether a cornerback prospect adds a durable option after the present injury clears. The same distinction applies to Olivine’s receiving absences and Canalave’s injured backs.
Give the offense a useful next answer

Eterna has allowed 137 points and scored 157. Its thirty-four sacks taken, including seven at Pastoria, make protection one of the clearest investigations on this sheet. I would compare Lapras, Eiscue and the other linemen directly, then assess whether a receiving outlet changes the quarterback’s available answers. A new blocker and a reliable short target can address related problems through different jobs.

Canalave has produced 1,190 passing yards and 128 points. That deserves a broader passing-game review than simply circling a quarterback on the board. The receiving options, protection and intended distribution of work belong in the same conversation. With Gabite and Nidoking unavailable now, the club also has a visible reminder to examine how its rushing plan survives absences. Those are connected personnel questions, and the draft should be judged by the improvement it can plausibly supply.

Mauville’s 2,743 passing yards have produced only 162 team points. I want a careful look at rushing help and protection before another offseason is spent admiring yardage that does not become enough scoring. University of Mauville’s Shuckle will receive local attention, naturally. The 66–94 band warrants evaluation; familiarity with the university does not settle how the prospect would block for this particular offense.
The league-wide first meeting

The table names primary comparisons rather than confirmed vacancies. It uses current production and availability, without assuming future trades, free-agent signings or draft order. Each club should revisit the priorities after the season and after it knows which players it will retain. The prospect cards below identify useful comparisons in the current visible class. No rookie named here can repair a Week 15 absence.

body.title: First scouting questions for all 32 clubs

Protect the productive passing game while testing whether a new runner can broaden the offense. A prospect’s listed position alone cannot settle the blocking problem.

Put the front-seven candidates through run assignments first. The offense also needs fewer difficult passing downs; both lines deserve a direct comparison.

articles.title: Injury Report: Sunyshore loses Gardener and FLOAT SZN before Rustboro
articles.dek: Canalave adds another rushing absence; Fortree and Pewter suffer long defensive losses; the full league recovery comparison.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Sunyshore loses two contributors before Rustboro

Serp Gardener is newly listed out two weeks and FLOAT SZN one after Sunyshore’s 17–0 win over Canalave. The Starseekers host Rustboro next, then visit Mossdeep. Those reported durations make the next two matchups a useful planning horizon, although an actual return still requires confirmation. The injury entries establish availability changes, not a new starting order or the exact play on which either injury occurred.

Sunyshore’s shutout deserves credit on its own terms. Karson Jones now has to prepare for an 8–5 Rustboro club with a changed cornerback group and one fewer available rushing option. Gardener is a cornerback; FLOAT SZN is a halfback. The two absences affect different jobs, so a single broad statement about being short-handed would obscure the decisions the team actually needs to make.
Canalave’s rushing absences grow

Nidoking is newly out one week after the Sunyshore game. Gabite’s existing absence has counted down from fourteen weeks to thirteen. Canalave now hosts unbeaten Mossdeep after scoring no points last week. The reported injuries add to the difficulty of finding enough rushing production to support the passing game. The evidence confirms the unavailable players; it does not identify a replacement starter.

Olivine has two new offensive absences before hosting Vermilion: halfback Gabite is out one week and receiver Maractus two. Beedrill’s earlier long absence now stands at sixteen weeks. The Ironclads scored twenty-one at Blackthorn but allowed forty-one, so the injury changes arrive alongside work on both sides of the ball. Olivine’s Gabite and Canalave’s Gabite are separate players with different injury entries.
Defensive losses across the league

Sootopolis cornerback Kingdra is newly out five weeks after the 24–17 loss to Dewford. Fortree outside linebacker Banette has a new twelve-week absence, the longest new entry this week, while receiver Haunter is out four weeks. Pewter outside linebacker Mightyena is out nine weeks and tight end Heatmor two after the 17–9 win at Vermilion. These are new reported absences rather than routine recovery countdowns.

Lavender’s Dugtrio is out one week at cornerback before Celadon visits. Cianwood receiver Haunter is out five weeks after the win at Violet. Mahogany tight end Golduck is out four weeks ahead of Pewter. The two Haunter entries belong to different players and clubs; Fortree’s number 17 and Cianwood’s number 14 should remain distinct in any discussion of replacements.
Recovery updates and minor entries

Mr. Clanky’s counter has reached zero at Lavender. Frosmoth played quarterback in the win over Azalea, and the cleared recovery counter does not by itself establish which passer will receive the next start. Pastoria’s Oinkologne, Sandygast and receiver Watchog also moved from one reported week to zero. They should not be confused with the separate Watchog who carried eighteen times in Pastoria’s latest game.

A zero counter is an availability update. The recorded game reports establish appearances separately, and the next role remains a team decision.

Ninjaskamara remains out two weeks, Richard Furman three, Marshall Flock one and Luvrelle Revis one. Those four continuing absences have counted down from the previous issue. articles.title: Game of the Week: Saffron brings the pressure to Mt. Silver
articles.dek: Trent Scarboro’s 11–2 Psi Corps visit Connor McLarren’s 12–1 Reds. Two outstanding defenses meet two passing games that still have mistakes to correct.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Saffron has allowed seventy-nine points in thirteen games. Mt. Silver has allowed 105. Those are the first numbers I would hand anyone arriving late to this matchup, followed immediately by two others: Archam Manning threw two interceptions against Viridian, and Tic Thorpe threw two at Mahogany. Both quarterbacks won. This week, the other sideline has considerably more experience turning a difficult possession into a long afternoon.

The Psi Corps arrive at 11–2 after beating Viridian 56–6. The Reds are 12–1 after a 23–7 victory at Mahogany. Mt. Silver has secured its division; Saffron has secured a playoff berth and can take Kanto East with a win or tie, or a Vermilion loss or tie. The conference's leading clubs have more to settle than whether their seasons continue. Home field, a possible bye and the order of the contenders remain worth fighting over.

My pick is Mt. Silver 27, Saffron 24. It is the most difficult choice on the slate. Saffron has the stronger season-long defensive scoring record and just produced a far larger victory. I give the Reds a narrow advantage because Thorpe has two receivers coming off substantial, complementary production and gets the opportunity at home. That is a judgment about this matchup, with enough room for Saffron to make it look foolish.
Saffron can score without a long passing afternoon

The fifty-six points against Viridian came from several sources. Manning threw five touchdowns on fifteen completions and 218 passing yards. Dam Skattebo ran fourteen times for 155 yards and a touchdown, then caught another score. Jolt Train Ln returned punts sixty-five and seventy-seven yards for touchdowns. A defense preparing only for a series of long Manning drives would be preparing for a different game.

Skattebo gives Trent Scarboro a direct way to test the middle of Mt. Silver's defense. Saffron finished with 216 rushing yards on twenty-two attempts. Emmitt Smoth contributed forty-nine on five carries, an additional reason the Reds cannot treat the running game as one player's responsibility. The Psi Corps faced only four third downs, converting two. Their explosive gains repeatedly shortened the route to the next scoring opportunity.

Mt. Silver has a useful recent defensive response. Mahogany managed sixty-five rushing yards on twenty-three carries and converted two of thirteen third downs. The Frost's entire offense reached 202 yards. Saffron asks harder questions than Mahogany did, but the Reds have just demonstrated that they can win first and second down often enough to make a possession expensive.

The check for Saffron is straightforward: reach 120 rushing yards and win the turnover margin. The first target would preserve a credible choice for Manning rather than asking him to solve every down through the air. The second matters because the Reds can survive a modest rushing total if Jenings and Gyarzalez receive extra chances. Saffron's fifty-point margin against Viridian should not disguise the two Manning throws that ended with the opponent.

“I believe in these guys,” Trent Scarboro said. “That includes believing they can hear what we have to fix. We gave two possessions away. Against this team, every player has to understand how much work we're asking our defense to do when that happens.” His confidence comes with a shared obligation: an offense celebrating fifty-six still has to help the defense that has carried such a small points-allowed total.
Thorpe has two different receiving answers

Gregar Jenings caught seven passes for 160 yards at Mahogany. Tony Gyarzalez caught eight for 106. Together, they supplied 266 of Thorpe's 335 passing yards and both receiving touchdowns. Jenings scored on a thirty-yard deep-left throw. Gyarzalez's touchdown came on a ten-yard short-right pass early in the fourth quarter. Saffron has to defend more than one depth and more than one finish.

Those numbers also explain why I have not simply compared the last two winning margins and chosen the larger one. Mt. Silver moved the ball. Its problems were the possessions it gave back and the limited points it extracted from a sizable passing total. Thorpe completed twenty-four of thirty-seven, but the Reds lost a fumble as well as his two interceptions and converted three of nine third downs.

Saffron supplied three sacks against Viridian, all credited to NeMarcus Tare. The recent defensive sequence is imposing: zero points allowed to Fortree, three to Cinnabar, zero to Vermilion and six to Viridian. Four opponents have combined for nine points. That stretch earns the Psi Corps considerable confidence, while the trip to Mt. Silver tests how well the same approach handles a much more productive receiving pair.

The Reds' rushing total at Mahogany was fifty-one yards on thirteen carries. Raticate scored from one yard out, while Vibrava led their listed runners with thirty-two yards. Mt. Silver does not need to reproduce Saffron's 216 to win, but a game that makes every meaningful gain Thorpe's responsibility would give the visitors too many chances to attack the same problem.

Connor McLarren sounded pleased that Saffron's defense was attracting attention. “They've earned every compliment,” he said. “I imagine they'd rather hear those than have Gregar asking where the ball is. We'll see which conversation they get more of.” The smile belongs in the rivalry coverage. The answer will depend on whether the Reds finish the drives their receivers make possible.
Returns can change the argument immediately

Jolt Train Ln's two punt-return touchdowns are a special-teams warning with actual distances attached. The first covered sixty-five yards; the second seventy-seven. Those plays made an already productive Saffron offense still harder to keep within reach. Mt. Silver punted four times at Mahogany. Every unsuccessful Reds possession this week must include the task of ending with a safe exchange of field position.

It would be excessive to forecast another two return touchdowns simply because they happened last week. It would be equally careless to treat the returner as a footnote. A kickoff or punt can alter which offense is asked to make the next difficult decision. Saffron's seven returns gained 248 yards against Viridian, a substantial contribution to a game in which the Psi Corps ran fewer offensive plays than their opponent.

Mt. Silver's defense can make Saffron work longer than Viridian did if it limits those changes of field position and keeps Skattebo from repeatedly breaking the first line. The Reds forced eight Mahogany punts. Their two sacks were fewer than Saffron's three, yet the series of defensive stops was sustained. A game can belong to a defense without every possession ending in a spectacular individual play.
Availability and the fourth quarter

Josh Alakazam remains out eight weeks. Thorpe's performance and preparation must therefore be assessed as the work of Mt. Silver's available quarterback, with the recent production attached to his name. Saffron has no currently reported multiweek absence in this issue's injury report. Neither fact guarantees a particular workload; both define the availability entering the week.

For Mt. Silver, my checkable targets are no more than one Thorpe interception and at least three offensive touchdowns. The Reds reached three offensive touchdowns at Mahogany; repeating that total while cutting the giveaways would make better use of their receiving advantages. Limiting the interceptions would remove one of Saffron's clearest opportunities to turn its defensive strength into a short scoring assignment.

For Saffron, the winning route combines useful early runs, pressure without repeated explosive concessions, and an offense that retains the ball after the return team has done its work. The Psi Corps do not need to score fifty-six. They need to make Mt. Silver uncomfortable enough that the next Thorpe completion fails to settle the afternoon.

I expect Jenings and Gyarzalez to supply enough productive catches for the home team, and I expect Saffron to make almost every comfortable moment temporary. My 27–24 pick assumes the Reds correct enough of the three-giveaway game to preserve their final scoring opportunity. If Manning gets a second straight week of clean protection and Skattebo keeps moving the chains, Saffron can take that opportunity away before the last possession arrives.

articles.title: Rustboro’s deep shots meet Sunyshore’s changing secondary
articles.dek: Gibby Timmy’s two long touchdowns give Tyler Scarboro a reason to test the Starseekers immediately. Karson Jones must replace an injured cornerback and running back after a division-clinching shutout.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Rustboro threw two touchdown passes at Fortree. Both went deep left to Gibby Timmy, one for fifty-two yards and the other for fifty-nine. Sunyshore shut out Canalave the same week, then arrived at this matchup with cornerback Serp Gardener listed out two weeks and running back FLOAT SZN out one. Those facts give the Stone a clear question to ask early: can the Starseekers keep the dangerous receiver from deciding where this game is played?

Sunyshore has secured Sinnoh East at 10–3. Rustboro is 8–5, one game behind Petalburg in Hoenn West and currently holding the fifth conference seed. The Starseekers still have seeding ambitions, including the remaining pursuit of Mossdeep, while the Stone need results that keep both their division hopes and their wild-card position healthy. A division title gives Karson Jones a milestone to acknowledge. The next opponent makes the defensive personnel problem immediate.

I favor Sunyshore 30–20. Rustboro can create a much more demanding passing test than Canalave supplied in the 17–0 shutout. I also expect the Starseekers' offense to find opportunities against a defense that allowed Fortree twenty-three points. My forecast needs Sunyshore to recover some offensive efficiency while limiting the number of long Stone completions, a combination more demanding than last week's score initially suggests.
Gibby Timmy changes what a quiet series can become

The Archeops receiver caught three passes for 138 yards at Fortree. Two catches supplied 111 yards and two touchdowns, followed by successful one- and two-point tries. The other completion still gained twenty-seven. That distribution makes the passing threat unusually clear: even a small number of successful throws can move the Stone far enough to change a close game.

Shawn Watzon, the Porygon-Z quarterback, completed sixteen of twenty-four passes for 276 yards and two touchdowns without an interception. He also ran for thirty-eight yards and a score. Rustboro produced 409 total yards and converted four of nine third downs. Those are substantial signs of offensive progress, especially for a team that had recently scored seven against Mossdeep before beating Mauville seventeen–three.

The new name should not obscure the continuity of the player. Watzon is the same number thirty-seven Porygon-Z who delivered the Fortree production. His clean interception column matters against a Sunyshore defense that took the ball away twice through the air against Canalave. Rustboro did lose two fumbles, so the offense's possession record was less tidy than the quarterback's passing line.

Tyler Scarboro was more interested in the unfinished possessions than in decorating the two long throws. “A map can show you the scenic route,” he said. “That's wonderful if you're on vacation. We're trying to get the ball down the field before somebody takes it away. Gibby made that part pretty direct.” He returned quickly to the practical point: explosive catches become less useful when a later possession supplies the opponent with a fumble.

Sunyshore must make Watzon complete the less glamorous throws as well. SEARED BITE caught four passes for sixty-two yards. Shieldon and Lombre each added twenty-seven receiving yards. The Stone have alternatives when the defense gives the deep threat extra attention, but those options need to convert ordinary downs rather than waiting for another fifty-yard rescue.
Sunyshore won with defense doing the heavy work

The Starseekers allowed Canalave 116 total yards. Slowking completed seven of twelve passes for fifty-five yards and threw two interceptions. Canalave rushed thirty-three times for sixty-one yards, a difficult return on a large commitment. Sunyshore recorded four sacks and kept the Bulwark from scoring despite several chances created by the home offense's mistakes.

Ash Rothington's thirty-four-yard interception return supplied one of Sunyshore's two touchdowns. The other came on a four-yard short-right throw from DeZhaun Watzon to Scol Alexander. A twenty-six-yard field goal completed the scoring. The Starseekers gained 221 yards, with 163 through the air and fifty-eight on the ground. They won convincingly on defense while leaving room for a considerably better offensive afternoon.

Watzon threw two interceptions, and Sunyshore also lost a fumble. Karson Jones has reason to celebrate the division title and equal reason to demand that the offense reduce the burden on its defense. Rustboro's offense just showed it can turn three completions to one receiver into 138 yards. Giving that group extra possessions would make the replacement cornerback’s assignment considerably harder.

“We earned the division,” Jones said. “The standard goes up with it. Everybody knows who we are now. The players stepping in have to know we believe in them, and the offense has to play like it understands how to help them.” His confidence is part of the program's public identity. This week it comes with a specific task for the available cornerbacks, running backs and the quarterback.
The absences matter without predicting the replacement

Cornerback Serp Gardener's two-week absence and running back FLOAT SZN's one-week absence are confirmed entering the matchup. Future starting assignments remain unsettled. Sunyshore needs an available cornerback to help cover Rustboro's receiving group, while its offense replaces the runner who supplied thirty of the team's fifty-eight rushing yards against Canalave.

Running back My Way, Son remains out four weeks for Rustboro. The Stone need their available runners to sustain the ground game alongside the production their receivers are providing. Gibby Timmy's long catches and SEARED BITE's intermediate contribution are obvious items for Sunyshore's preparation, so Rustboro should expect the next defense to make the first preferred answer more difficult.

A sensible Starseekers response begins with keeping the receiver in front and forcing more completions per scoring drive. That does not prescribe an unseen private coverage call. It describes the result Sunyshore needs: reduce fifty-two and fifty-nine yards to a sequence of smaller gains, then make the Stone finish a third down without losing the ball.

Rustboro's best response is patience when the long route is covered. Philly ran for fifty-two yards, Watchog forty and Watzon thirty-eight at Fortree. The Stone accumulated 133 rushing yards. There is enough recent ground production to justify asking the defense another question before attempting the next deep throw, especially when a controlled possession can keep Sunyshore's offense waiting.
What the next result would establish

Rustboro's win at Fortree required a fourth-quarter response. The Skyhawks led 23–21 before Watzon hit Gibby Timmy for the fifty-nine-yard touchdown and found Philly on the two-point conversion. That is evidence of an offense capable of recovering under pressure. It also means the Stone spent much of a game against a three-win opponent without controlling the result.

Sunyshore offers a stronger test of whether the passing improvement can travel. The Starseekers have allowed 167 points through thirteen games and just recorded a shutout. Their missing cornerback is a meaningful opening for Rustboro, but the whole defensive record deserves consideration alongside the injury list. A single replacement cannot carry the entire explanation for whatever happens next.

For the Stone, my target is at least three completions of twenty yards or more. That would show the downfield threat survived the step up in opponent and give Rustboro enough territory to challenge the forecast. For Sunyshore, I want Rustboro below twenty-four points and a positive turnover margin. The latter requires the offense to contribute by keeping possession rather than simply waiting for another defensive takeaway.

The wider conference will watch both results in this race: Rustboro at Sunyshore and Petalburg at Pastoria. Dewford also travels to Hearthome. Those games can change the Hoenn West order and the group immediately behind the division winners. Sunyshore's title is already secured, while its pursuit of a better postseason position continues with Mossdeep visiting Canalave before their own meeting next week.

My thirty–twenty Sunyshore pick allows Rustboro some explosive success. I expect the Starseekers to answer with more productive offense than they managed against Canalave and enough defensive stops to keep the long catches from becoming the whole game. If Gibby Timmy gets behind the available coverage as readily as he did at Fortree, that ten-point margin can disappear in the time it takes one throw to arrive.

articles.title: Five tickets punched—and the wild-card branches that can leave ten wins short
articles.dek: Sunyshore clinches its division, Saffron and Blackthorn qualify, and Mossdeep has a bye route. Ellis Quill follows nine possible final-week wild-card branches.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Sunyshore has won Sinnoh East. Saffron and Blackthorn have booked playoff places. Mossdeep can secure the Hoenn–Sinnoh bye this week. Those are substantial developments, but I keep returning to the clubs around the seventh seed: four games remain, and a team can improve its record while discovering that a rival’s result has made the route narrower.

The Starseekers’ 17–0 win over Canalave secured their division even though Pastoria beat Eterna. Sunyshore is 10–3; Pastoria, at 6–7, can still reach ten wins. That possible tie belongs to Sunyshore. The Starseekers already have four division victories, while Pastoria can finish with only three. Karson Jones has earned a title before the visits from Rustboro and the trip to Mossdeep. The conference’s first seed remains available.

Below are two different kinds of chart. The first describes exact Week 15 conditions for Mossdeep to clinch the bye. The larger wild-card tree asks what happens in a specified possible final-week situation, including ties and three different combinations of qualifiers. Its assumptions are printed beside it. It shows a route the schedule permits; it is not a forecast that those earlier results will happen.
Five invitations are already secured

Saffron’s 56–6 win over Viridian and Blackthorn’s 41–21 win over Olivine lifted both clubs to eleven wins. The remaining schedule cannot produce enough qualifying rivals to push either out. Their division titles are still open. Saffron leads Vermilion by four wins, but the clubs split their meetings and the Volts can still finish 11–6. Blackthorn leads Lavender by three, with their second meeting reserved for the final week.

Seven clubs qualify in each conference: four division winners and three wild cards. The division winners take seeds one through four; the first seed alone gets the opening-round bye. The X, Y and Z markers indicate a secured berth, division or first seed respectively. A club sitting seventh today has a place in the current order and still has work to do.
Mossdeep’s bye: follow both results

Mossdeep visits Canalave at 13–0, while 10–3 Sunyshore hosts Rustboro. An Eclipse victory plus any Starseekers result short of a win clinches the first seed. A Mossdeep tie also suffices if Sunyshore loses. Every other combination leaves the bye open after Week 15. Sunyshore still visits Mossdeep in Week 16, which is why a three-win lead cannot be treated as permission to skip the calculation.

For example, a Blackthorn win and a Lavender win would leave both able to finish with twelve victories. The Dragons have won the first meeting, but the Wails could split that series in Week18 and bring division records into the argument. Blackthorn therefore needs the specified help for the straightforward route above.

Petalburg’s opportunity is striking after the shutout at Mossdeep. Beat Pastoria and receive a Veilstone win or tie against Mauville, and the Pride secure entry. That would leave the Hoenn West title to be settled against Rustboro and Dewford. Petalburg swept the Breakers, but still visits the Stone in Week17. A berth would give Norman’s club a definite achievement while those division games retain their significance.
A final-week wild-card tree with three different answers

Here is a possible Kanto–Johto finish that shows why the last wild-card place demands more than a list of current records. Assume Violet wins its remaining four games. Assume Lavender beats Celadon and Blackthorn but loses to Cerulean and Violet. Both would finish 10–7. Give Olivine wins over Vermilion, Pewter and Cianwood before its final trip to Azalea. Give Vermilion wins over Mahogany and Fuchsia after the assumed Olivine loss. The Volts and Ironclads would each enter Week18 at 9–7.

Cerulean, meanwhile, beats Azalea and Lavender before losing to Saffron, entering its home finale against Vermilion at 8–8. These are demanding assumptions, especially Violet winning out and Lavender beating Blackthorn. They are useful because the resulting finale contains a genuine choice of qualifiers. None of these clubs is being awarded those earlier victories in the current standings.

body.text: The harshest branch is the first: Vermilion and Olivine both win. Lavender, Vermilion, Olivine and Violet all finish 10–7, and Violet misses. The league first resolves the division order, where Lavender holds the division-record advantage. It then applies the wild-card procedure separately for each available place. Violet cannot claim that matching the other clubs’ overall records is sufficient.

Change only Olivine’s finale to a tie or loss while Vermilion wins, and Violet gets in with Lavender and Vermilion. Change Vermilion’s finale to a tie while Olivine wins, and the qualifiers become Lavender, Violet and Olivine. If both finales end tied, the Ironclads’ assumed Week15 win over the Volts gives Olivine the head-to-head advantage at 9–7–1 for the last opening. That is a concrete reason to care about Vermilion’s trip to Olivine now.

Cerulean can win its finale and still miss under this setup. If Olivine also loses, the Tide, Volts and Ironclads finish 9–8 while Lavender and Violet stand at 10–7. Vermilion wins the division-record comparison with Cerulean; Olivine then wins its head-to-head comparison with Vermilion. The third wild card goes to Olivine. A win over the team immediately ahead can be valuable without resolving the entire multi-team tie.
The games that can change the setup immediately

The example begins with three consequential Week15 games: Vermilion at Olivine, Cerulean at Azalea and Viridian at Violet. A different result changes the later arithmetic and calls for a different tree. Lavender’s home game against Celadon supplies another important starting condition. Travis Scarboro’s club has won four straight and occupies the fifth seed at 8–5; the example deliberately gives it difficult late losses to show why those wins already banked matter.

In Hoenn–Sinnoh, Rustboro and Dewford are both 8–5, Canalave is 7–6, and Mauville and Pastoria are 6–7. Rustboro visits division champion Sunyshore; Dewford visits Hearthome; Canalave receives unbeaten Mossdeep. Eterna, also 8–5, holds Sinnoh West and hosts Lavaridge. The Thorns’ 10–3 loss at Pastoria kept that division close enough for Canalave’s remaining games to influence both the title and the wild-card field.

My immediate attention is on Olivine–Vermilion and Rustboro–Sunyshore, alongside the obvious Saffron–Mt. Silver headline. Each changes the position of a contender while affecting another team’s route. Four games remain. The charts describe what particular results secure and who qualifies in a defined finish; the next set of final scores will decide which branches deserve another week of attention.
